title: Develop
sub: A complete set of professional tools, non-destructive from end to end.
lead: White balance, tone, curves and colour mixing, AgX tone mapping, and highlight recovery from the raw file's own headroom.

title: RAW decoders
sub: Three decoders, three tone mappers, and a different look from each.
lead: Every other developer decides how your raw is decoded and never mentions it again. Chili RAW puts the decoder in Settings, routes each file to the right one by default, and re-renders your edited thumbnails when you switch — so comparing them is honest rather than flattering.

title: Culling
sub: Cull a large shoot from the keyboard.
lead: Culling is the part of the job that decides how the rest of it feels. The grid is built for it: rate and flag from the keyboard, narrow with a filter band that never hides anything by accident, and put the likely keepers first when you don't know where to start.

title: Burst stacks
sub: Collapse a burst of frames into a single tile.
lead: Shoot a run of frames a fraction of a second apart and the grid fills with near-duplicates. Stacks collapse each burst into a single tile so you scan scenes instead of frames, then open one only when you want to choose inside it. Nothing is moved, renamed or deleted — it is a way of looking.

title: The Loupe
sub: The loupe Aperture had, with focus peaking added.
lead: A loupe you drag across the thumbnails, showing real pixels under the cursor without opening anything. Aperture's was the best tool it had, and it left with it in 2015. This one follows the same idea and adds the part Aperture never had: it can tell you whether the focus actually landed.

title: Masking
sub: Mask any part of a photo, eleven different ways.
lead: A local adjustment is only as good as the selection under it. Chili RAW gives you three families of selection — drawn, computed and detected — and lets you combine any of them into a single mask with add, subtract and intersect.

title: AI masking
sub: Select skies, subjects, and objects in a single click.
lead: One click for the sky, the subject, a single object, or a slice of the scene by distance. Every model runs on-device — no image ever leaves the machine, and nothing runs until you download the model you want.

title: Portrait editing
sub: Adjust skin, eyes, lips, and hair — each on its own.
lead: Select a person with one click, then narrow the selection to the part you actually want to work on. Lift the skin without dulling the eyes, warm the lips without warming the face, brighten hair without lifting the background. Each part is a normal mask, so the same local adjustments apply inside it — this is targeted editing, not a beauty filter.

title: Repair
sub: Remove dust, blemishes, and whole objects.
lead: Three tools, in order of how much of the picture they touch. Heal and Clone fix specks and small blemishes with a circle and a source. Dust detection finds the specks for you and proves each one against neighbouring frames. Generative Remove takes out the things that are too big for a circle.

title: Bokeh
sub: Blur the background the way a fast lens would.
lead: A depth map of your own photograph drives a defocus that runs in scene-linear light, before the tone curve — which is what keeps a specular highlight as a bright disc instead of a grey smudge. It is a lens property, not a selection, so it lives beside the tone controls rather than in the masking tab.

title: Lens corrections
sub: Correct distortion, vignetting, and fringing with real lens profiles.
lead: Every lens bends straight lines, darkens the corners and splits colour at the edges. Chili RAW reads the correction tables your camera writes into the file, and ships the Lensfun calibration database for the lenses that have none — then names the one it matched, so you can see what is being applied and to which axis.

title: Versions
sub: Several edits of one photograph, and none of them a copy.
lead: Try the warm grade and the cold one. Keep the crop you are not sure about. A version is a separate set of develop settings on the same file — instant to switch, free on disk, and comparable side by side with the zoom locked together.

title: LUTs
sub: Your own .cube files, and the stocks that ship with it.
lead: Link the LUT folder you already have and it is scanned recursively, subfolders and all. Import the ones you use constantly and they become swatches. Then dial any of them back with Intensity, because a look at 35% is usually the one you wanted.

title: Film Labor
sub: Run your photos through a real film pipeline.
lead: Film Labor renders your photograph the way film would have: exposed onto a negative, scattered inside the emulsion, printed onto paper, then viewed under a light. It is not a filter laid over the image — each stage is measured from datasheets, and the order of the chain is physics rather than preference.

title: Pixels
sub: Add type, borders, and date stamps without opening another app.
lead: The last step of a picture is often the smallest one — a border, a caption, a glowing date in the corner — and it is absurd that it usually means launching a second application. Pixels is a layer canvas that sits on top of your developed photograph, non-destructive until the moment you export.

title: Catalog & backups
sub: Your edits live beside your photos. The index is disposable.
lead: Edits, masks and versions are written to sidecars next to the originals, which are never modified. The catalog on top of that is a fast, searchable index you can throw away and rebuild — and a Vault copies the whole lot to another drive as plain, restorable files.

title: Search
sub: Search by filename, keyword, place, or person — or by what's actually in the picture.
lead: By its name, by the keywords you wrote, by the place it was taken, by who is in it — or by what it looks like, when you cannot remember any of that. Everything is indexed on your own machine, and none of it needs the photos to be imported anywhere.

title: People
sub: Find every photo of a person, without uploading anything to the cloud.
lead: Scan a library once and the same face is grouped together wherever it appears. Name a group and that person becomes a filter you can combine with everything else — the shoot, the place, the rating. Your photos stay on your disk: detection, grouping and naming all run on your Mac, and nothing is sent to a server.

title: Geo Tag
sub: Put your photos on a map, and find them by where you were.
lead: Half the frames from a trip have coordinates and half do not, depending on which body shot them. The Geo Tag view fixes that: a map beside a table of every photo, so you can place a frame with a click, search for a place by name, or paste a coordinate onto a whole selection — written as standard GPS metadata every other app can read.

title: EXIF / IPTC
sub: Read your camera's data, and write your own.
lead: Every frame arrives carrying what the camera recorded — body, lens, aperture, ISO, the moment it was taken. What it does not carry is what the photo is of, who made it, and who owns it. This view shows the first and lets you write the second, across one photo or two hundred.

title: Export
sub: Export in any format, at any size, with full control.
lead: Export is where the work either survives or quietly doesn't. Chili RAW renders at full resolution and resamples afterwards, sharpens the pixels that actually get written, and shows you the finished file at actual size before you commit to a batch of two hundred.

title: Video
sub: Play, cull, and grade your clips beside your photos.
lead: The clips from a shoot live in the same folders as the frames, so Chili RAW treats them like the photographs they sit next to — they appear in the grid with a duration badge, they rate and flag with the same keys, they play full screen, and they take a colour grade that is applied per frame on export.

title: Detail
sub: Sharpen what is there, and rebuild what is not.
lead: One panel, split by a divider. Above it is capture sharpening — the pass every raw file needs, already at 40 when the photo opens. Below it are the four that deal with what the sensor did not record cleanly: Apple's raw noise reduction, and three models you download once and run on your own Mac.
